beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. A friend of mine dumped his meeting notes into an AI and said, make me a slide deck. What came back was eighteen slides of walls of text. Here is the three-move way from rough notes to a deck people can actually read.

props.text: Make my notes into a slide deck.
props.triggerWords: Make my notes into a slide deck
props.replacementWords: Turn my notes into a slide deck, one move at a time

beats.narration_text: Three terms. An outline: the skeleton of the deck, one line per slide. A slide: one idea on one card — a headline, not an essay. And the polish: cutting every slide down until it reads from the back row. That’s all you need for this film.

beats.narration_text: Start with the goal. A pile of rough notes in — a five-slide deck out, every slide clean enough to read from the back row. No walls of text, no tiny print. That is a deck without the slog.

beats.narration_text: So he pasted the notes and asked for the whole deck at once. Out came eighteen slides in about a minute — and every single one was a wall of text. Asked for everything at once, the AI did not know what mattered. So it kept everything.

shot.visual_intent: One big slide card lands covered in many text lines; stacked cards sit behind it; the label 'all at once' lands; terracotta dots flag the walls of text.

beats.narration_text: Here’s why. A slide is not a page. The moment a slide fills with words, the room reads the slide instead of listening to you. And an AI building the whole deck at once guesses what matters most — it cannot know what you would cut.

shot.visual_intent: A big slide on a screen; three audience dots at the side; their sight lines draw to the slide, not the speaker; the label 'walls get read' lands.

beats.narration_text: Move one: the outline. Before a single slide exists, ask the AI for a one-line-per-slide skeleton — the whole deck, no prose. Then you do the most important job in this film: read it, fix it, approve it. The outline is the contract, same as in The long game.

shot.visual_intent: The outline card lands; its five slide rows draw in; a terracotta check stamps your approval; the label 'move one: outline'.

beats.narration_text: Move two: one slide per prompt. The AI drafts slide one — only slide one — with the outline beside it. Small enough to check in one sitting, because you read it before slide two starts.

shot.visual_intent: The outline card slides left; slide one drops in; an arrow draws card to slide; the label 'move two: one slide'; a check lands on the slide.

beats.narration_text: Then the polish. Read each slide and cut the words — a headline plus a few short lines, nothing more. And the words you cut are not lost: they move where they belong, into the speaker notes — the lines only you see.

beats.narration_text: Last move: the back-row test. Step back from the screen and read the slide. If you cannot catch the headline in a few seconds, it is still too full. Cut again, then step back once more.

beats.narration_text: Make it a habit. Outline first. One slide per prompt. Polish last. Anything you would show a room is a deck without the slog — build it in three moves.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I’m turning rough notes into a five-slide deck. Don’t build any slides yet. First, draft a one-line-per-slide outline from my notes, then wait for my approval. My notes: [paste them here]. Then check two things yourself. Does the AI give you an outline, not slides? And is every note on it — nothing missing, nothing invented?
